name: Memory and Storage
blurb: HBM, DRAM, SSDs, and the storage tiers behind training runs.

items.name: HBM3E
items.note: The US HBM supplier; HBM3E ships in H200 and Blackwell platforms

items.name: HBM3E / HBM4
items.note: The leading HBM supplier and primary memory partner for NVIDIA's datacenter GPUs

items.name: VAST Data
items.note: All-flash data platform widely deployed in GPU clusters, including CoreWeave's

items.name: WEKA
items.note: Parallel filesystem for AI training I/O; feeds GPU clusters at hyperscale customers

reading.body:
High-bandwidth memory is a duopoly with one domestic fallback: SK Hynix leads HBM supply for NVIDIA's datacenter GPUs, and Micron is the only US-headquartered alternative, with both now shipping HBM3E into the H200 and Blackwell platforms.

The dependency matters for AI training because HBM sits directly on the GPU die and determines how fast the processor can move data during computation. A training run's throughput is bounded first by that memory bandwidth, not by raw compute counts. The four items here cover two layers: on-package memory from SK Hynix and Micron, and the cluster-level storage systems, VAST Data and WEKA, that stage datasets and checkpoints for GPU clusters at hyperscale and cloud customers like CoreWeave.

What this data does not cover is DRAM and SSD supply chains, which the page description mentions but which have no entries here. The four items are verified to September 2026, so transitions beyond HBM3E, including HBM4, are listed only in passing for SK Hynix without detail on availability or volume. The record is a starting point for the memory layer, not a complete map of it.
